Meta (all authors)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — SWE-Together, a 109-task multi-turn benchmark reconstructed from real user-agent coding sessions with an anchored, state-conditional LLM user simulator and rubric-based correctness scoring; seven frontier models compared on a common harness (opencode) against a reference-patch baseline

No SDD approach. Harness: opencode (version not stated). Models: Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-2.7. Baseline: original reference patch ('Reference'). Models used for the user simulator, viability screener, task-generation agent, rubric judge and message tagger not stated

Per task package: original session record, initial user instruction (first turn), pinned execution environment and repository commit, deterministic verifier artefacts (tests), task-specific user-simulation prompt with decomposed user intents and trigger conditions per feedback turn; frozen weighted task rubric (behavioural goals) for scoring. No artefact prescribed to the evaluated agent beyond the user's messages

Replay: agent receives the original initial request; after each completed agent turn the trajectory is summarised and the simulator chooses one action (no-op, question, redirect, new-requirement, check-external); message actions are injected as user turns; final repository state scored. Construction: deterministic filtering -> LLM viability screening -> sandboxed task construction by a task-generation agent
None in the evaluated loop (user simulated by an LLM). Four human annotators judged simulated vs real trajectories for simulator validation
Full workflow of each model on the opencode harness through multi-turn simulated sessions
Not classifiable; authors' wording: tasks 'cast as fixed, single-turn instructions' vs users who 'reveal intent incrementally'; an agent may 'require a detailed specification'
Existing code bases: repository-level tasks on public GitHub repositories restored at a pinned commit

109 tasks from 11,260 raw sessions (0.97%): DataClaw 2,228 -> 29, Pi-staging 2,397 -> 23, Hyperswitch 784 -> 9, SWE-chat 5,851 -> 48; reference patch available for 93 tasks; 2 replicates per task per model; 29.9k-74.0k output+reasoning tokens per task. Repository sizes Not stated
Mixed open-source repositories from real coding-agent sessions (including a production payments codebase, Hyperswitch); domains and languages not detailed

Judge score in [0,1] = weighted share of frozen rubric goals met; with threshold tau = 0.85: pass@1 (marginal per-run success), stable solve rate SSR (mean of 2 replicates >= tau), pass^2 (both replicates >= tau); MeanJudge (continuous). Deterministic verifiers provide executable evidence
None

User Correction (simulated): N_correction + 0.2 N_nudge per trial from a multi-label tagger over simulator messages, averaged over replicates then tasks; used as proxy of the corrective steering an agent elicits
Intent Coverage (simulator fidelity) = 0.70 intent recall + 0.30 scope precision; Turing pass rate of the simulator (share of judgments choosing the simulated trajectory as real)

Automatic: agentic rubric judge (Phase 1 derives a weighted rubric per task offline, may consult the reference patch; Phase 2 returns binary met decisions with evidence per goal; host-side validator checks coverage, weights and score consistency); deterministic verifiers; LLM tagger for User Correction; intent decomposition and matching for Intent Coverage; tokens and time per task. Manual: four annotators, forced two-alternative choice on 156 trajectory pairs (312 judgments). Judge not validated against humans

opencode harness, 109 tasks, k = 2 replicates. Authors' success threshold is task-level (judge >= 0.85); no configuration-level criterion. Tasks: 109 SWE-Together tasks. Configurations: 7 models. Baseline: original reference patch scored by the same frozen rubric (93 tasks). Held constant: harness (opencode), task package and pinned environment, frozen rubric per task, simulator anchored to the original session (intent order and trigger conditions). Acceptance: agentic rubric judge with deterministic verifier evidence, threshold 0.85. Repetitions: 2 per task per model. Human intervention: none (simulated user); serving infrastructure of endpoints not controlled

Claude Opus 4.8 best on all four correctness metrics (pass@1 63%, MeanJudge 0.801) and lowest User Correction (1.38), about 15 pp below the reference pass rate; GPT-5.5 second (0.763) and most efficient (29.9k tokens, 10.7 min); MiniMax-2.7 last on all correctness metrics and most correction (2.17). User Correction strongly inversely correlated with pass@1 (Pearson -0.92), SSR (-0.84), MeanJudge (-0.93) across the seven models; cost only weakly coupled to capability. No significance tests or confidence intervals for the model comparison

Distinguished the models (MeanJudge 0.630-0.801) with a consistent ordering across metrics; pass^2 vs pass@1 exposes run-to-run variance (2 replicates). Simulator consistency: Intent Coverage 0.68-0.72 across cohorts; Turing pass rate 46% (95% CI 40.5-51.6%), not distinguishable from real users. Reference scores below 100% because rubrics include process requirements (about 35% of unsatisfied goals), incomplete reference patches and imperfect human solutions. Latency may depend on serving infrastructure. Limitations stated: simulator cannot interrupt, edit files or see the UI; best for clearly defined goals and measurable outcomes

Limitations: user simulator cannot interrupt agent turns, edit files or use visual information; works best with clear goals and measurable outcomes; limited coverage of ambiguous, open-ended tasks and qualitative user behaviours. Gaps: static single-turn benchmarks miss interaction quality and user effort; evaluation should also measure how much corrective steering an agent elicits
